summary: The longest chapter in the book, and everything falls apart in it. A woman pours expensive perfume over Jesus's head and is criticized for waste; he says she has prepared him for burial. Judas goes to the chief priests. At the Passover meal Jesus says one of them will hand him over, then gives them bread and a cup and calls them his body and blood. In Gethsemane he asks for the cup to be taken away and his closest three fall asleep three times. He is arrested, everyone runs, and while he stands before the council saying plainly who he is, Peter stands in the courtyard below swearing he never knew him.
whyItMatters: Mark builds this chapter so that Jesus is finally, openly identifying himself upstairs at the exact moment his best friend is denying him downstairs. It is the last and sharpest of Mark's sandwiches, and the whole book has been walking toward it.

context.author: Anonymous; early tradition names Mark, recording Peter's preaching — and this chapter contains the most damaging material about Peter in any gospel
context.audience: Greek-speaking readers outside Judea; Mark keeps the Aramaic 'Abba' and explains the Passover timing
context.setting: Bethany, an upper room in Jerusalem, the Mount of Olives, Gethsemane, and the high priest's house — all within one night
context.literaryForm: Passion narrative, the oldest continuous block of gospel tradition, with Mark's sandwich technique framing the trial and the denial

outline.heading: The plot, and the anointing
outline.note: A woman's extravagance framed by two scenes of men arranging a murder

outline.heading: Preparing the Passover
outline.note: A man carrying water, an upper room already furnished

outline.heading: One of you will hand me over
outline.note: Each of them asks 'surely not I?'

outline.heading: Bread and cup
outline.note: Four sentences that shaped two thousand years of Christian worship

outline.heading: You will all fall away
outline.note: Peter insists otherwise; so do all of them

outline.heading: Gethsemane
outline.note: Distress, a request that is refused, and three rounds of sleeping disciples

outline.heading: Arrest
outline.note: A kiss, a severed ear, everyone fleeing — including a young man who gets away naked

outline.note: False witnesses who cannot agree, then a direct question and a direct answer

outline.heading: Denial — inner half resolved
outline.note: Three times, the second rooster, and Peter breaks

keyVerses.text: wherever this Good News may be preached throughout the whole world, that which this woman has done will also be spoken of for a memorial of her.
keyVerses.why: A promise kept every time this chapter is read — and her name is not recorded.

keyVerses.text: This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for many.
keyVerses.why: The interpretation he gives his own death, spoken before it happens.

keyVerses.text: Abba, Father, all things are possible to you. Please remove this cup from me. However, not what I desire, but what you desire.
keyVerses.why: A prayer that states the request honestly and then submits — and the request is not granted.

keyVerses.text: I am. You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of the sky.
keyVerses.why: After a whole book of silencing, he answers plainly — under oath, at the moment it will kill him.

questions.question: Was the perfume really worth that much?
questions.answer: Three hundred denarii is close to a year's wages for a labourer. Nard was imported from the Himalayan region, and the jar was sealed — breaking it meant it could not be resealed or used sparingly. So the objection is not petty; this is an enormous sum poured out in seconds. What Mark does with it is place the scene between the chief priests plotting and Judas going to sell him. One woman gives away a fortune; a friend takes money.

questions.question: 'You always have the poor with you' — is that a dismissal of helping the poor?
questions.answer: It has been used that way and it does not survive reading. The phrase quotes Deuteronomy 15:11, whose full sentence is: the poor will never cease from the land, therefore I command you to open your hand wide to your brother. Anyone who knew the passage would hear the command inside the quotation. Jesus's actual point is in the second half of the verse — 'you will not always have me' — which names this as a unique moment, not a policy.

questions.question: Why does she anoint his head, and why does he take it as burial preparation?
questions.answer: Pouring oil on the head is how kings were anointed in Israel — the word Messiah means anointed one. So the act is a coronation, performed by an unnamed woman in a leper's house, days after crowds shouted about David's kingdom. Jesus accepts it and redirects it: bodies were anointed for burial too. He takes the kingship gesture and says it is a funeral rite. That is the whole argument of the second half of this gospel in one act.

questions.question: Why is a man carrying a water jar a useful sign?
questions.answer: Because carrying water was women's work, so a man doing it stood out in a crowded festival city. Whether this was prearranged or foreknowledge, Mark does not say — the same ambiguity attaches to the colt in chapter 11. What the detail does establish is that the location was kept quiet, which matters given that one of the men at the table was already negotiating with the authorities.

questions.question: What does 'this is my body' mean? Christians seem to disagree sharply.
questions.answer: They do, and the disagreement is old and serious. Catholic teaching holds transubstantiation: the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood while the appearances remain. Orthodox tradition affirms a real change and generally declines to define the mechanism. Lutherans hold that Christ is truly present in and with the bread and wine. Reformed traditions hold a real but spiritual presence received by faith. Others, following Zwingli, read it as a memorial. What every side agrees on: he said it at a Passover meal, where the bread and herbs were already understood to make a past deliverance present to the people eating, and he told them to keep doing it.

questions.question: What is a covenant, and why 'new'?
questions.answer: A covenant is a binding relationship with terms, sealed by a ceremony — the arrangement between God and Israel at Sinai was sealed with blood thrown on the people (Exodus 24:8). Jeremiah 31:31 promised a new covenant, written on hearts rather than tablets. So Jesus is using the language of the founding moment of his nation and saying the sealing blood this time is his own. It is an enormous claim, made quietly, over dinner.

questions.question: What is 'the cup' he asks to be taken away?
questions.answer: In the Hebrew scriptures the cup is regularly an image for an allotted portion, often of God's judgment (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15). He used it in 10:38 asking James and John whether they could drink it. So his request is not simply about pain or death — it is about drinking down what that cup contains. Notice the shape of the prayer: he states that all things are possible, asks plainly for what he wants, and then submits. He does not pretend not to want it.

questions.question: What does 'Abba' mean, and why keep the Aramaic?
questions.answer: It is the ordinary Aramaic word a child used for their father — warm and familial, though not baby talk as is sometimes claimed. Mark preserves the actual sound and translates it immediately, as he does elsewhere. Paul reports the same word being used in prayer by Greek-speaking congregations in Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6, which suggests it stuck because people remembered Jesus using it.

questions.question: If the disciples were asleep, who heard the prayer in Gethsemane?
questions.answer: A fair question, and readers have answered it several ways. Mark says they fell asleep, but the sleeping is described in rounds with Jesus returning between them, so there is waking in the gaps. He also prayed aloud, a short distance away — verse 35 says he went forward a little. Others suggest he told them afterward. Mark does not address it, which is itself worth noting: a writer inventing the scene would probably have tidied this, and would almost certainly not have made his own sources the men who slept through it.

questions.question: Who is the young man who runs away naked?
questions.answer: Nobody knows, and only Mark includes it. It is a strange, specific, slightly humiliating detail that advances nothing — which is exactly why it has attracted attention. A long-standing guess is that it is Mark himself, quietly signing the account, in the way artists sometimes paint themselves into a crowd. Others read it as an image of total abandonment, since the previous verse says they all fled: even the last one clinging on escapes by leaving everything, including his clothes. There is no way to settle it.

questions.question: Was this trial legal?
questions.answer: By the standards later recorded in Jewish law, several things about it are irregular — capital cases at night, on the eve of a festival, with a verdict reached the same session, and conviction on testimony that verse 56 says did not agree. Two cautions: those rules are documented in sources written down later, so applying them directly is uncertain, and Mark may be describing a hurried hearing rather than a formal trial. What Mark clearly wants you to see is that they sought witnesses to put him to death first and looked for grounds second.

questions.question: Why is 'I am' enough to convict him?
questions.answer: Because of what he adds. Asked whether he is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed, he says 'I am' — a phrase that also echoes the divine name in Exodus 3:14 — and then combines Daniel 7:13 with Psalm 110:1: the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, coming with clouds. Claiming to be Messiah was not itself blasphemy; plenty of men had. Claiming to sit enthroned beside God was another matter. The high priest tears his clothes, the prescribed response to hearing blasphemy, and no further witnesses are needed.

questions.question: Why does Mark cut back and forth between the trial and Peter?
questions.answer: It is the sharpest use of his sandwich technique. Verse 54 puts Peter in the courtyard, then the trial runs upstairs, then verse 66 returns to him below. The two scenes happen simultaneously and comment on each other: Jesus is asked who he is and finally says it plainly, at the cost of his life; Peter is asked the same kind of question by a servant girl and denies it three times to save his skin. If the early tradition is right that this book carries Peter's preaching, then the most damning account of Peter in the New Testament came from Peter.
